summary: Describes HTTP header fields a TLS-terminating reverse proxy can use to pass client certificate information from a mutual TLS connection to the origin server in a common way. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A doorman checks your ID and tells the people inside who you are, using a standard note.

questions: how to pass client certificate through reverse proxy
subtitle: Passing client certificate information through a reverse proxy in HTTP.

tldr.problem: When a TLS-terminating reverse proxy (TTRP) receives a mutually authenticated TLS connection, the origin server behind the proxy needs to know about the client certificate, but the TLS connection to the origin is separate.
tldr.mechanism: The TTRP adds Client-Cert and Client-Cert-Chain HTTP header fields to each request sent to the origin, containing the client certificate information from the original TLS connection.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now use client certificate information in a standard, predictable way for access control, audit logging, and token binding without proprietary header fields.

facts.label: Certificate encoding
facts.value: Base64-encoded DER X.509, delimited by colons

today: RFC 9440 is an Informational RFC published in July 2023 and has not been obsoleted. It codifies existing practice for conveying TLS client certificate information in HTTP when using reverse proxies.

sections.title: The Reverse Proxy Problem
sections.content: Many HTTPS services sit behind a reverse proxy that terminates TLS connections from clients. The proxy handles the encrypted connection with the client, then forwards requests to an origin server in a protected network. The client's TLS connection only goes to the proxy, not to the origin server. If the client authenticated with a certificate (mutually authenticated TLS), the origin server needs that certificate information for its application logic, such as access control, audit logging, or binding tokens to the certificate. At present, different implementations use different, non-standard header fields to convey this information, making interoperability difficult.
sections.eli5: The doorman sees your ID, but the people inside don't. The doorman needs to tell them who you are in a way they can understand.

sections.title: The Client-Cert and Client-Cert-Chain Headers
sections.content: RFC 9440 defines two new HTTP header fields. The Client-Cert header field contains the end-entity certificate from the client in DER-encoded X.509 format, represented as a base64-encoded Byte Sequence delimited by colons. The Client-Cert-Chain header field, optional, contains the certificate chain used to validate the client certificate as a list of base64-encoded certificates. The order matches the TLS order: intermediate certificates first, then the root (which may be omitted if the origin server already knows it). Both headers are used only in HTTP requests to the origin, never in responses.
sections.eli5: One header has your ID card written in a special secret code. Another header has the official stamps proving it's real, in the same order they were checked.

sections.title: Processing Rules at the TTRP and Origin
sections.content: The TTRP performs the following steps for each request on a mutually authenticated TLS connection. First, it places the client certificate in the Client-Cert header field. Second, if configured, it places the validation chain in Client-Cert-Chain. Third, and critically, it removes or overwrites any Client-Cert or Client-Cert-Chain header fields that arrived in the original client request, preventing a malicious client from spoofing the headers. Requests over a non-mutually-authenticated TLS connection MUST be sanitized by removing both headers. The origin server uses the Client-Cert header to determine the client certificate and can make access control decisions based on it. When using the Client-Cert value to select a response, the origin must either mark the response uncacheable with Cache-Control: no-store or send Vary: Client-Cert to limit caching to requests with identical Client-Cert values.
sections.eli5: The doorman gives everyone the same kind of note about their ID. The doorman also erases any note the person tried to make before entering, so nobody can fake it.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content: The size of certificate data in the Client-Cert and Client-Cert-Chain headers can affect HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 header compression. Multiplexing requests from many clients over one connection may reduce compression efficiency, though increasing the dynamic table size or sending field values as literals rather than table entries can mitigate this. Additionally, recipients may need to allow larger maximum header sizes, since certificate data is substantial. Some TLS implementations do not retain client certificate information when resuming sessions; implementations unable to provide consistent values should either disable resumption for connections with client certificates or initially omit the headers if resumption might lose the values.
sections.eli5: The notes are big and can slow down fast sending of many notes together. Also, sometimes the fast connection needs to remember who you are, and it might forget.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The Client-Cert and Client-Cert-Chain headers enable a TTRP and origin server to function as a logical HTTPS endpoint from the client's perspective. Misuse outside this intended deployment can undermine TLS client certificate authentication protections. Both producing and consuming the headers SHOULD be configurable, with the default being to not use them, requiring explicit opt-in. Critically, origin servers MUST only accept these headers from a trusted TTRP in a trusted path; backend servers are responsible for rejecting the headers if they arrive from an untrusted source. A TTRP MUST sanitize incoming requests by removing or overwriting any existing instances to prevent clients from controlling the header values. Communication between the TTRP and origin server must be secured against eavesdropping and modification.
sections.eli5: The doorman must actually erase fake notes from anyone trying to trick the people inside. And the people inside must trust the doorman and only listen to notes from him.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: RFC 9440 is an Informational RFC published in July 2023, codifying existing practice. It is not a standards track document but represents IETF consensus on a pattern deployed in reverse proxy architectures, content delivery networks, and load balancers. The header fields are registered as permanent in the HTTP Field Name Registry, enabling stable interoperable use.
sections.eli5: This is an official note about how things work now. Everyone agrees this is the right way to do it.
